newsitem.title: INDIA: TEXT-India's Chidambaram, RBI chief meet bankers.
newsitem.headline: TEXT-India's Chidambaram, RBI chief meet bankers.

text.p: Following is a statement issued by the Indian government on Tuesday after a meeting between Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, Reserve Bank of India Governor C. Rangarajan and the chiefs of public sector banks.

"Finance Minister had a meeting on 9th December 1996 lasting over four hours with the Chief Executives of the Public Sector Banks. The meeting was attended by the Governor, Reserve Bank of India, Finance Secretary, all the deputy Governors of the Reserve Bank of India, Additional Secretary (Banking) and other senior officials of the Finance Ministry, Reserve Bank of India and the Banks. The meeting discussed the prevailing credit scenario and the issues of reduction in non-performing assets, priority sector advances with special reference to rural credit and credit to weaker sections, modernisation and customer service and improving the internal control system of the banks.

In his observations, the Finance Minister said that the central issue facing the banks today is to meet the genuine credit needs of the different segments of the economy in an efficient manner. He referred to the rising mismatch between growth in deposits and growth in bank credit. In this context, he referred to the perceptions voiced in certain quarters regarding non-availability of credit. The phased reduction in CRR announced by RBI in the latest credit policy is likely to release about 85 billion rupees into the system. The easy liquidity position is reflected in the softening of the call money rates and also reduction in the PLR of most banks. The clients have a feeling that banks

In the context of the easy liquidity situation and the favourable climate created by the latest credit policy, the Finance Minister emphasised the need for the banks to actively and agressively compete for good credit-worthy clients.

Some of the Chief Executives referred to the special features in the banking system where commercial decisions involving an element of risk were taken and emphasised the need to provide an environment which will encourage such decisions. Finance Minister assured that the institutional mechanism will be strengthened to provide protection for bonafide commercial decisions, while at the same time ensuring that cases of malfeasance are speedily brought to book.

The bank chairmen assured that the liquidity position is now comfortable and that they will take measures to remove the perception about the lack of availability of credit and would simplify the appraisal and sanction procedures/documentation so that all proposals for enhancement or new facilities from credit-worthy borrowers would be cleared within two to eight weeks of their receipts.

The Governor in his remarks pointed out that while deposit growth had been strong in the current year, credit growth had been sluggish. He emphasised that deposit growth would continue to remain strong in the coming months and with lower cash reserve requirement and with government borrowing programme almost completed, the lendable resources of banks would expand considerably. Banks should therefore plan for a larger credit expansion. Stressing on the importance of bringing down non-performing assets, the Governor wanted banks to put in place a clear and acceptable mode for arriving at compromises. As regards house keeping, the Governor mentioned that there has been considerable improvem

There was a detailed discussion on the issue of Non-Performing Assets and recovery of bad debts. It was noted that gross NPAs of public sector banks as proportion of outstanding credit has come down from 24.8 percent in 1993/94 to 17.1 percent in 1995/96. It was also noted that the incremental NPAs on fresh bank credit since introduction of prudential norms in 1992/93 were about 3.5 percent. While expressing satisfaction at these trends, Finance Minister observed that the amount of credit locked up in NPAs at nearly 400 billion rupees is still extremely high and measures need to be taken to reduce this hangover of the past so that the NPAs are brought down to sustainable and acceptable l

The functioning of the Debt Recovery Tribunals and the need to expedite their work was also discussed in detail. It was pointed out that these Tribunals were set up in recognition of the need to provide a machinery for quick enforcement of bank securities. Because of organisational, administrative and legal problems, these Tribunals have not been able to start effective functioning. So far, notifications for setting up six Tribunals in Delhi, Jaipur, Calcutta, Bangalore, Ahmedabad and Chennai had been issued while notifications for Patna and Guwahati are likely to be issued shortly. Tribunals at Jabalpur and Mumbai are in the process of being set up. Finance Minister emphasised the need

The performance of banks in the priority sector lendings was also discussed in detail. It was noted that while in the first six months of the current year, lending to priority sector is more than the prescribed 40 percent of the net bank credit, the performance needed to be sustained during the remaining part of the year. Some suggestions were also made for the integration of the multifarious rural employment schemes and the need to involve banks in formulation of schemes involving bank credit. It was clarified that a committee set up by RBI has recently finalised its report on integration of credit linked employment schemes.

Several other issues including modernisation and induction of technology, internal control systems including house keeping and customer service was discussed in detail. It was pointed out that the banking system has so far invested about 6 billion rupees on computerisation. About 1,500 bank branches have been fully computerised. This had improved customer service in the areas of cash acceptance, updation of pass books, issue of demand drafts etc. It had also improved credit related services and helped in house keeping including inter-branch reconciliation.

The banks are now moving from the "stand alone" computerisation to on-line network systems. The shared payment network system in Bombay involving 185 ATMs belonging to 35 banks is likely to be operationalised by February 1997.
The bank chairmen assured the Finance Minister of their utmost efforts in improving customer service and in putting in place an effective internal control system."
